*A core principle behind all Indivisible events is a commitment to nonviolent action. We expect all participants to seek to de-escalate any potential confrontation with those who disagree with our values.*

**Resolutions express the opinion, intent, or will of the Town Council on a particular topic. They typically address matters of a special or temporary nature or handle administrative acts.
    Examples:
        Establishing advisory committees.
        Supporting a particular cause or communicating with another governmental unit.
        Directing the Town Manager to take certain administrative actions.
    Characteristics:
        Can often be acted upon in a single reading.

description:
Due to popular demand, we will be holding an evening postcarding party. We are contacting more of the Virginia and Pennsylvania voters who are holding elections this November: since off-year elections are often viewed as a harbinger for the midterms, it is important that we send a message about the strength of the Democratic ticket heading into 2026. 

We will be writing cards to infrequent voters who are Democrats or Democratic-leaning, which will be mailed in mid-October for maximum impact. Both of these elections will be watched very closely as bellwethers for the 2026 midterms, and a strong showing by Democrats will make a strong statement against Trump and MAGA.

Virginia's Republican governor is term-limited, so that's an open seat, and the Democrats have a strong candidate who has a good chance of winning if we get our voters out: it also has a razor-thin majority in the state legislature that we need to preserve. 

In Pennsylvania, there are three State Supreme Court justices in a retention election: if they are not retained, the PA Supreme Court will be deadlocked, with two Democratic and two Republican justices. Since it is very likely that there will be litigation after the 2028 election, it is vital that we hold on to this court.

As always, I'll bring postcards, scripts, stamps, & writing supplies: you bring your enthusiasm for the Democratic ticket. I will provide snacks: feel free to bring any food you'd like to share as well (but that's not required.)

RSVP here, and we’ll let you know how to join this party. Invite your friends, too. Think about it: if you help get a voter to the polls, that is an important step towards creating a more inclusive and equitable government and society. Looking forward to seeing you!

His personal biography, from the Palestinian West Bank to New Orleans, where he personally experienced the effects of gun violence and Hurricane Katrina, to Indianapolis, Fady Quadoura is one of Indiana’s most inspiring political leaders.  

**Senator** Qaddoura’s **record as a public servant is unrivaled.** Before entering the senate,  and during his tenure as Indianapolis comptroller, he was credited with balancing the city’s $1.2 billion budget without tax increases after a decade of structural budget deficits that exceeded $55 million annually, securing five consecutive credit ratings enhancements from national credit agencies, lowering the overall city debt, and playing a significant role in executing many of the city's operational and economic development strategies. In 2018, he was named CFO of the Year by the Indianapolis Business Journal. 

 It is a summer of deep discontent in Indiana. As K-12 students start the school year, and college campuses kick off the fall semester, join us for this meeting.

description:
Dhan B. Basnet, Esq., and Karan Phambota will share powerful stories and lead a Q&A discussion. 

He is the founder of the Law Office of Dhan B. Basnet, PLLC. Mr. Basnet has been practicing immigration law in the U.S. since 2015. Prior to that, he practiced law as an advocate for about seventeen years in Nepal. He has also co-authored a book titled “General Administrative Law of Nepal.”

Mr. Basnet received Masters of Law (LL.M.) from the University of Washington. He also has Master of Arts (M.A.) in political science and Bachelors of Law (B.L.) from Tribhuvan University, Nepal. As an immigrant himself, Mr. Basnet fully understands the stress, anxiety, and frustration of going through the complicated immigration process. He speaks English, Hindi, Nepali, and Urdu languages. He has been successfully counseling and representing clients in removal proceedings, naturalization applications, family-based petitions, U Visas, Asylum, K visas, VAWA applications, and employment-based visas.

Karan Phambota is an immigration attorney and partner at the Law Office of Dhan B. Basnet, PLLC, a Seattle based immigration law firm. Karan has been practicing law since 2019. Prior to practicing immigration law, Karan practiced family law for almost five years. 

Karan Phambota obtained his bachelor’s degree from Washington State University in 2016. In 2019, he graduated from Seattle University School of Law with a Juris Doctorate. Mr. Phambota comes from an immigrant family and can understand the stress that comes with the immigration process. He speaks English, Punjabi, and Hindi.

title: Registration Repair 2.0
description:
In July, we mailed over 1,000 letters—and we’re doing it again! This September, we're coming together to write letters to North Carolina voters whose registrations may be at risk. These voters could be denied a regular ballot if their information isn’t corrected by October 10th.  We will supply the letters, envelopes, pens and return address labels. Please bring first class letter stamps if you can. 

Why This Matters

The North Carolina State Board of Elections requires voter registrations to include either a driver’s license number or the last four digits of the Social Security number. Even a small mismatch—like a typo—can flag a registration as “incomplete.” That means the voter will be forced to vote provisionally, which can increase the risk of their vote not being counted.
Right now, over 100,000 North Carolinians have registrations flagged as incomplete—including 10,000 in Wake County alone.

Let’s make sure they know how to fix it before it’s too late. Join us September 13th—your letters make a difference!

description:

title: Immigration Crisis in Indiana – Challenges, Impacts, and Action
description:
Join us for an important virtual event presented in partnership with Indivisible of Central Indiana, ACLU of Indiana, Coalition for our Immigrant Neighbors (COIN), and Kathy Souchet-Downey with Congressman Andre Carson’s office. We’ll explore the legal, social, and economic realities facing our immigrant neighbors in Indiana—and discuss what’s being done to support justice and inclusion.

Since January 20, 2025, ICE has carried out nearly 1,400 administrative arrests in Indiana, an almost 80% increase compared to the same period last year. About a quarter of these arrests in June involved people with no criminal convictions or charges, while nationally, the share of non-criminal arrests has risen sharply. Meanwhile, Indiana officials have begun entering 287(g) agreements with federal immigration enforcement—partnerships that allow certain local law enforcement officers, after ICE training, to perform federal immigration duties such as checking immigration status, issuing detainers, and initiating deportation proceedings. As of mid-2025, four Indiana law enforcement agencies have signed on, though some are not yet active pending training. Critics warn these agreements encourage racial profiling, erode trust in police, and target individuals without criminal histories.

At the same time, the Pentagon has notified Congress of a plan to use Camp Atterbury in Indiana to detain immigrants, though exact timing and logistics remain unclear. Civil liberties advocates caution that this could intensify due process concerns and further strain trust between immigrant communities and the government.

Yet Indiana communities—especially in Indianapolis—are thriving in part because of immigrant contributions. Refugees and new Americans have launched businesses, revitalized neighborhoods, and supported local schools and industries. Community estimates from the Burmese American Community Institute suggest there are about 30,000 Burmese immigrants in the greater Indianapolis area, many of whom are essential to the region’s economic growth.

During this event, speakers will:
• Break down how heightened ICE enforcement and local law enforcement agreements are affecting immigrant communities in Indiana
• Share first-hand insights from ACLU, COIN, and local organizers about developments.
• Highlight the positive contributions and challenges of immigrant residents in central Indiana
• Offer tangible ways to engage, advocate, and support humane immigration policy

This session is essential for anyone committed to protecting immigrant rights and understanding what’s happening in our state. We encourage you to register and submit questions in advance. Zoom link will be sent after you register.

title: Getting Out the Vote for Virginia and Calling Swing Districts to Save Scientific Research Funding
description:
The state of Virginia has elections in 2025 for the office of Governor, Lieutenant Governor and for the House of Delegates. Because this is an odd-year election, fewer people are likely to vote and efforts to increase turnout are likely to be impactful. We will be calling South Asian voters in Virginia to encourage them to vote in the November elections. 


We will be calling South Asian voters in swing districts represented by Republicans to ask them to contact their representatives about the huge funding cuts the Trump administration is proposing to the NIH and NSF. They plan to cut 38% from the NIH and 55% from the NSF and have already withheld $3.8 billion dollars in science funding. Furthermore, billions of dollars in funding to universities and research centers has been delayed relative to previous years and the administration plans to further reduce the number of grants approved by paying money for multiyear grants up-front instead of year by year. The Senate Appropriations Committee has marked up an NIH-friendly bill that would increase funding for FY 2026 and stop the change to multiyear funding. We will be asking voters to contact their house members in support of similar provisions
